# Why I Stopped Buying Cheap Tools

Hey everybody, welcome back to the workshop. Today I want to talk about something that cost me a lot of money before I figured it out, and that's buying cheap tools.

Now, I'm not here to tell you that you need the most expensive brand on the shelf. You don't. But there's a difference between affordable and cheap, and learning that difference is what this whole video is about.

[pause]

Let me start with a story. A few years ago I bought a bargain drill from a discount bin. It looked fine. It had a nice case, a couple of batteries, and a bright orange handle. The first weekend I used it, the chuck started wobbling. By the third project, it wouldn't hold a bit straight at all. So I bought another one, the same model, thinking I just got unlucky. That one lasted about a month.

Here's the thing nobody tells you. When a tool fails, it doesn't just cost you the price of the tool. It costs you the afternoon. It costs you the board you just split. And honestly, it costs you a little bit of the joy you get from making things.

## What actually matters

So what should you look for? I've got three things I check before I buy anything now.

First, how does it feel in your hand? Pick it up. If the store lets you, squeeze the trigger, turn the knobs, feel the weight. A good tool feels balanced. A cheap one usually feels hollow, like a toy that's pretending to be serious.

Second, can you get parts for it? This one surprised me. Some companies sell replacement brushes, blades, belts, and batteries for years. Others disappear after one season. If I can't find a spare part online, I walk away, because that tool is basically disposable.

Third, what are other people saying after a year? Not the first week. Everything is great in the first week. I look for reviews from folks who've owned it long enough to beat it up a little. Those are the reviews that tell you the truth.

## Where I do save money

Now, I don't want you to think I spend big on everything. I absolutely don't. Clamps, for example. You can never have enough clamps, and the inexpensive ones work just fine for most jobs. Same with chisels, honestly. A modest chisel that you sharpen well will beat a fancy one you never sharpen.

Hand saws are another place you can save. Pick up an old saw at a yard sale, clean the rust off, give it a fresh edge, and it'll outlast anything you'd find in a plastic blister pack.

The rule I follow is pretty simple. If a tool has a motor or a battery, I buy the best one I can reasonably afford. If it's a simple hand tool, I buy used or modest and put my effort into maintaining it.

[pause]

So that's my take. Buy fewer tools, buy better tools, and take care of the ones you have. Your projects will come out cleaner, and you'll spend a lot less time fighting your equipment.

If this was helpful, let me know in the comments what tool you regret buying cheap. I read every single one. And I'll see you in the next video.
